label: Chapter 4
title: The Hill Difficulty and Giant Grim

blocks.p: Now I saw still in my dream that they went on until they came to the place where Simple, Sloth, and Presumption had lain sleeping when Christian went by on his pilgrimage; and there they were, hanged up in irons a little way off, on the other side of the road.
“Who are those three men,” Mercy asked their guide, “and why are they hanging there?”

“Those three were men of very bad character,” said Great-heart. “They had no mind to be pilgrims themselves, and they hindered everyone they could. They were for sloth and folly, and whoever they could talk round they made the same; and besides that, they taught them to presume that they would do well enough in the end. They were asleep when Christian went by; and now, as you go by, they are hanged.”
“But could they persuade anyone to think as they did?”

“Yes. They turned several out of the way. There was Slow-pace, whom they persuaded to do as they did. They won over one Short-wind, and one No-heart, and one Linger-after-lust, and one Sleepy-head, and a young woman named Dull, to turn out of the way and become like them. Besides this, they spread an evil report of your Lord, persuading people that he was a slave-driver. They spread an evil report of the good land too, saying it was not half so good as some pretended. They began to run down his servants, and to call the very best of them meddlesome, troublesome busybodies. Further, they could call the bread of God husks; the comforts of his children, fancies; and the travel and labor of pilgrims, things to no purpose.”

“Well,” said Christiana, “if they were like that, I shall never mourn for them. They have only what they deserve, and I think it is a good thing they hang so near the highway, where others can see them and take warning. But wouldn’t it have been well to have their crimes engraved on a plate of iron or brass and left here, on the very spot where they did their mischief, as a caution to other bad men?”
“So it is,” said Great-heart, “as you will see if you go a little way toward the wall.”

“No, no,” said Mercy. “Let them hang, and their names rot, and their crimes stand against them forever. I count it a great mercy that they were hanged before we came this way; who knows what they might have done to poor women like us?” Then she turned it into a song:

v: Now hang there, you three; hang, and be a sign
to all who would against the truth combine;
and let whoever follows fear this end,
if to the pilgrims he is not a friend.
And you, my soul, of all such men beware,
who stand against the holy everywhere.

blocks.p: So they went on until they came to the foot of the Hill Difficulty, where their good friend Mr. Great-heart again took the chance to tell them what had happened there when Christian himself went by. First he brought them to the spring. “Look,” he said, “this is the spring Christian drank from before he went up the hill. Then it was clear and good; but now it is dirty with the feet of some who do not want pilgrims to quench their thirst here.” [Ezek. 34:18]
“And why so spiteful?” said Mercy.

“Still,” said their guide, “it will do, if it is drawn up and put in a clean, good vessel; then the dirt sinks to the bottom and the water comes clear by itself.” So Christiana and her companions had to do just that. They drew the water up and put it in an earthen pot, let it stand until the dirt had settled, and then drank.

Next he showed them the two byways at the foot of the hill, where Formalist and Hypocrisy had lost themselves. “These are dangerous paths,” he said. “Two men were cast away here when Christian came by. And though, as you see, these ways have since been blocked with chains, posts, and a ditch, there are still those who would rather take their chances here than take the trouble to climb this hill.”
“’The way of transgressors is hard,’” said Christiana. [Prov. 13:15] “It is a wonder they can get into those paths without breaking their necks.”

“They will risk it. And if any of the King’s servants happen to see them, and call out to them, and tell them they are on the wrong road, and warn them of the danger, they answer back with abuse: ‘As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you; we will do whatever comes out of our own mouths.’ [Jer. 44:16-17] And if you look a little further, you will see that these paths are fenced off well enough, not only by the posts and the ditch and the chain, but by a hedge besides; and still they choose to go there.”

“They are idle; they don’t like to take pains, and uphill going is unpleasant to them. So what is written is fulfilled in them: ‘The way of the slothful man is like a hedge of thorns.’ [Prov. 15:19] They would rather walk into a snare than climb this hill, and the rest of the way to the City.”

Then they set out and began to climb the hill, and up the hill they went; but before they reached the top, Christiana began to pant. “This hill takes your breath, I must say,” she said. “No wonder those who love their ease more than their souls choose a smoother way for themselves.”
“I have to sit down,” said Mercy; and the smallest of the children began to cry.
“Come, come,” said Great-heart, “don’t sit down here; the Prince’s arbor is only a little way above.” Then he took the little boy by the hand and led him up to it.

When they reached the arbor, they were very glad to sit down, for they were all hot and sweating. “How sweet is rest to those who labor,” said Mercy. [Matt. 11:28] “And how good the Prince of pilgrims is, to provide such resting places for them! I have heard a great deal about this arbor, but I never saw it before. Only let us beware of sleeping here; for from what I have heard, that cost poor Christian dear.”
Then Mr. Great-heart said to the little ones, “Come, my fine boys, how are you? What do you think of going on pilgrimage now?”

“Sir,” said the smallest, “I was almost beaten out of heart; but I thank you for lending me a hand when I needed it. And now I remember what my mother told me, that the way to heaven is like going up a ladder, and the way to hell is like going down a hill. But I would rather go up the ladder to life than down the hill to death.”
“But the proverb says going downhill is easy,” said Mercy.
“The day is coming,” said James (for that was his name), “when, in my opinion, going downhill will be the hardest thing of all.”
“That’s a good boy,” said his guide. “You have given her the right answer.” Mercy smiled; but the little boy blushed.

“Come,” said Christiana, “will you have a bite to eat, to sweeten your mouths while you sit here and rest your legs? I have a piece of pomegranate here, which Mr. Interpreter put into my hand just as I was leaving his door. He also gave me a piece of honeycomb and a little bottle of cordial.”
“I thought he gave you something,” said Mercy, “because he called you aside.”

“Yes, so he did. But it shall still be as I said it would be when we first left home: you shall share in all the good I have, because you so willingly became my companion.” Then she gave to them, and they ate, Mercy and the boys together. “Sir,” said Christiana to Mr. Great-heart, “will you eat with us?”
“You are going on pilgrimage,” he answered, “and I shall soon be going back. May what you have do you much good; at home I eat the same every day.”

When they had eaten and drunk and chatted a little longer, their guide said, “The day is wearing on. If you think it best, let us get ready to go.” So they got up to go, and the little boys went in front. But Christiana forgot to take her bottle of cordial with her, and had to send her little boy back for it.
“I think this is a losing place,” said Mercy. “Here Christian lost his scroll, and here Christiana left her bottle behind. Sir, what is the cause of it?”

“The cause,” their guide answered, “is sleep or forgetfulness. Some sleep when they should stay awake, and some forget when they should remember; and this is exactly why, so often at the resting places, some pilgrims come away the losers in some way. Pilgrims should watch, and remember what they have already received in the midst of their greatest joys; but for want of this, their rejoicing often ends in tears, and their sunshine in a cloud. Witness what happened to Christian in this very place.”

When they came to the spot where Mistrust and Timid had met Christian, to persuade him to turn back for fear of the lions, they saw what looked like a scaffold, and in front of it, facing the road, a broad plate with a verse written on it, and underneath, the reason the scaffold had been raised in that place. The verse was this:

v: Let him who sees this stage take heed
to what his heart and tongue have done,
or else he’ll come to this indeed,
as some did here in days long gone.

blocks.p: The words underneath the verse were: “This stage was built for the punishment of those who, through timidity or mistrust, are afraid to go further on pilgrimage. On this stage Mistrust and Timid were both burned through the tongue with a hot iron, for trying to hinder Christian in his journey.”

“This is much like the saying of the Beloved,” said Mercy: “’What shall be given to you, or what shall be done to you, you false tongue? Sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper.’” [Ps. 120:3-4]

So they went on until they came within sight of the lions. Now Mr. Great-heart was a strong man, and not afraid of a lion; but when they came up to the place where the lions were, the boys who had been walking in front were glad enough to cringe behind, for they were afraid of the lions, and they stepped back and fell in at the rear. At this their guide smiled and said, “How now, my boys? Do you love to go in front when no danger is near, and love to come behind as soon as the lions appear?”

As they went up, Mr. Great-heart drew his sword, meaning to make a way for the pilgrims in spite of the lions. Then there appeared a man who, it seems, had taken it on himself to back the lions, and he said to the pilgrims’ guide, “What is the reason for your coming here?” The man’s name was Grim, or Bloody-man, because of all the pilgrims he had slain; and he was of the race of the giants.
“These women and children are going on pilgrimage,” said the guide, “and this is the way they must go; and go it they shall, in spite of you and the lions.”
“This is not their way, and they shall not go this way. I have come out to stand against them, and to that end I will back the lions.”
Now to tell the truth, because of the fierceness of the lions and the grim bearing of the one who backed them, this road had lately lain almost unused, and was nearly grown over with grass.

“Though the highways have been unused before now,” said Christiana, “and though travelers in times past were made to go by byways, it must not be so now that I have risen. Now ‘I am risen a mother in Israel.’” [Judg. 5:6-7]
Then Grim swore by the lions that it would be so, and told them to turn aside, for they should have no passage there.
But their guide made straight for Grim first, and laid into him so heavily with his sword that he forced him to retreat.
“Will you kill me on my own ground?” said the one who had tried to back the lions.

“It is the King’s highway we are standing in,” said Great-heart, “and it is in his way that you have set your lions. But these women and these children, weak as they are, shall hold on their way in spite of your lions.” And with that he gave him another straight blow and brought him to his knees. With this blow he broke his helmet as well, and with the next he cut off an arm. Then the giant roared so hideously that his voice frightened the women; yet they were glad to see him lying sprawled on the ground. Now the lions were chained, and so could do nothing on their own. So when old Grim, who had meant to back them, was dead, Mr. Great-heart said to the pilgrims, “Come now, and follow me, and no harm shall come to you from the lions.” They went on, though the women trembled as they passed the lions, and the boys looked as if they would die; but they all got by without further hurt.

Now they were within sight of the Porter’s lodge, and they soon came up to it; and they made the more haste after this, because it is dangerous to travel there at night. When they reached the gate, the guide knocked, and the Porter called, “Who is there?” But as soon as the guide said, “It is I,” he knew his voice and came down, for the guide had often come there before as a conductor of pilgrims. When he had come down he opened the gate, and seeing the guide standing right in front of it (he did not see the women, who were behind him), he said, “How now, Mr. Great-heart? What is your business here so late tonight?”

“I have brought some pilgrims,” he said, “who by my Lord’s command are to lodge here. I would have been here some time ago, if I had not been opposed by the giant who used to back the lions; but after a long and hard fight I have cut him down, and brought the pilgrims here in safety.”
“Won’t you come in and stay till morning?” said the Porter.
“No. I will go back to my Lord tonight.”

“Oh, sir,” said Christiana, “I don’t know how to be willing for you to leave us on our pilgrimage. You have been so faithful and so loving to us; you have fought so bravely for us, and been so hearty in counseling us, that I shall never forget your kindness.”
“If only we could have your company to our journey’s end!” said Mercy. “How can poor women like us hold out on a road so full of troubles as this one, without a friend and defender?”
“Please, sir,” said James, the youngest of the boys, “be persuaded to come with us and help us, because we are so weak, and the way is so dangerous.”

“I am at my Lord’s command,” said Great-heart. “If he appoints me to be your guide the whole way, I will gladly wait upon you. But here you failed at the start: when he told me to come this far with you, you should have begged him to let me go all the way through with you, and he would have granted your request. As it is, I must withdraw for the present. And so, good Christiana, Mercy, and my brave boys, farewell.”
